chunk_findings.detail: `_case_end` never uses the new `_comment` check, so a `#` comment inside a case arm is still walked instead of skipped. For input `echo "$(case x in x) # esac )<newline>git push origin main;; esac)"`, bash runs `git push origin main` (`# esac )` is a comment); the guard's `_case_end` treats the comment text `esac` as the closing `esac`, returns before the real `esac`, and `_find_body` then closes the outer `$()` at the `)` inside the comment, dropping `git push origin main`, so `F.check` misses it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_case_end

chunk_findings.detail: The new nested-substitution branch only handles backticks and `$()`, not process substitution `<(...)` / `>(...)`; the same gap remains in `_case_end`. Given `echo "$(cat <(echo ); git push origin main)"`, bash executes `git push origin main`, but `_find_body` sees the process substitution's closing `)` as the closing `)` of the outer `$()` and truncates the substitution body before `git push`, so `F.check` returns None.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_find_body

chunk_findings.detail:
The new `_comment` helper is only wired into `_find_body`; `_case_end` still has no `#` branch, so a comment inside a `case` arm is scanned char-by-char. Given `echo "$(case x in x) # esac)
git push origin main
;;
esac)"`, bash executes `git push origin main` in the case arm, but `_case_end` sees the commented `esac` as the closing keyword, drops `depth` to 0, and returns with `k` on the following `)`. `_find_body` then takes that `)` (also inside the comment) as the end of the enclosing `$(...)`, so the scanned body stops before `git push origin main` and `F.check` returns None for the forbidden command.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_case_end

chunk_findings.detail: The diff adds `<(`/`>(` handling only inside `_find_body` (via `_sub_body`), but `_scan` is the top-level scanner that builds the initial substitution bodies from the raw command. For input `cat <(git push origin main)`, `_scan` never passes the leading `<` to `_find_body`, so the process substitution body `git push origin main` is not recorded as a command; the whole string stays one command headed by `cat`, and `F.check` returns None even though bash runs `git push origin main`. The new regression test only covers a `<(...)` nested inside an outer `$()`, not this top-level case.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/forbidden.py:_scan
